title: Why cloud services go down: 10 causes behind outages

 Why cloud services go down: 10 causes, from bad configuration changes to expired certificates and heat waves, with real incidents at Microsoft, AWS, Google and Meta
 1 / 12 List slides What causes a cloud outage? 10 real incidents show how services fail List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 12, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 An email inbox looks like one product, but it rests on many layers that most users never see. Getting a message into Outlook depends on networks that route traffic, systems that confirm who is signing in and digital certificates that prove a server is genuine. It also depends on data centers with steady power and working cooling. A fault in any one of those layers can make the whole service look broken, even when the mailbox itself is intact.
 Outlook.com and Exchange Online run on Microsoft $MSFT 's cloud infrastructure. That shared foundation lets Microsoft serve many customers from common pools of servers and networks. It also means a single problem in a shared component can reach several services at once. When Outlook stops loading, other Microsoft 365 apps such as Teams can be affected by the same fault.
 Microsoft reports Microsoft 365 incidents on its service health pages. Those pages are the first place to check when the question is why Outlook is down. Other large providers publish their own status updates and post-incident reports. Those write-ups explain what failed and why in each provider's own words.
 This slideshow looks at why cloud services go down through 10 causes. They are a selection, not a complete or ranked list. Some start with a routine task that goes wrong, such as a command issued during a network change or a certificate that was allowed to expire. Others come from software that behaves unexpectedly under load, from deliberate attacks or from the physical world, including heat waves and lightning.
 Each slide pairs one cause with a real incident and the company's own explanation of it. Several of those incidents happened at Microsoft . Others happened at AWS, Google $GOOGL Cloud, Oracle $ORCL and Meta $META , or involved CrowdStrike $CRWD software on Windows machines. Those cases show how a type of failure works, not how Outlook itself went down.
 Each slide also covers how companies try to prevent outages of that kind. The defenses differ by cause. They range from staged rollouts and certificate tracking to traffic filtering, throttling and backup power. A provider that guards against one failure can still be exposed to another.
 Faulty configuration changes 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A single faulty configuration change can take down many cloud services at once, because shared infrastructure carries traffic for all of them. On Jan. 25, 2023, a problem in Microsoft $MSFT 's Azure wide-area network disrupted Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook and Teams.
 Microsoft tied the disruption to a command issued during a planned network change. In other words, the trouble began with scheduled engineering work on the network itself.
 A configuration change adjusts how systems are set up, rather than the software code they run. Examples include updating routing tables, changing firewall rules, adjusting a server setting or editing an address range. Engineers make changes like these routinely to add capacity, fix problems and retire old equipment.
 Most of those changes pass without incident. The risk lies in scope. A wide-area network links data centers to each other and to the wider internet. When a change disrupts that layer, every service running on top of it can feel the effect at the same time.
 That is how one network command could affect both email and team chat. Outlook.com and Exchange Online sit on Microsoft 's cloud infrastructure. Users see separate apps, but those apps share the same underlying network. A fault in that shared layer does not stop at the boundaries between products.
 Configuration errors can also spread quickly. A change pushed to many devices can take effect within moments. By the time monitoring systems flag the trouble, the bad setting may already be active across a large footprint.
 Cloud providers guard against this with staged rollouts. Instead of applying a change everywhere at once, engineers apply it to a small slice of the system first. They watch for errors before widening the change step by step. If something breaks, the damage stays contained to that first slice.
 Rollback is the other half of the safeguard. A rollback plan lets engineers reverse a change and return systems to their last known good state. Automated validation tools can also check a command against set rules before it runs. That step catches some errors before they reach live equipment.
 The January 2023 incident also shows why the cause of an Outlook outage is often invisible from the inbox. Mailboxes and the apps that open them can be intact while the network beneath them fails. From the user's side, both problems look the same: messages stop loading.
 Bad software updates 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A single defective software update can disable a vast number of computers almost as soon as it ships. Automatic delivery sends the same flaw to every connected machine at once.
 On July 19, 2024, CrowdStrike $CRWD pushed a defective content update for its Falcon sensor, the company's security software for Windows. Microsoft $MSFT estimated that about 8.5 million Windows devices were affected.
 This was not a failure inside Outlook's servers or Microsoft 's cloud email systems. The update crashed endpoint machines. Those are the laptops, desktops and servers that organizations and individuals run on their own.
 That distinction matters when working out why email or another app stopped working. A cloud service can be healthy while the device used to reach it is broken. A worker whose computer will not start cannot open Outlook, even when nothing is wrong with the service behind it.
 Security tools receive frequent updates so they can recognize new threats. Vendors deliver those updates automatically to keep protection current without waiting on each customer. That speed is the purpose of the design. It also means a mistake travels exactly as fast as a fix would.
 Security software typically runs with deep access to the operating system. That access lets it watch for malicious activity across the whole machine. It also means a defect at that level can take down the entire computer, not just a single program.
 One common defense is the update ring. Machines are divided into groups that receive a change in sequence. A small first ring, often made up of internal test systems, gets the update before anyone else. Later rings receive it only after the earlier group has run cleanly.
 Microsoft 's own tools for managing Windows updates let IT administrators arrange devices into rings of this kind. The approach trades some speed for safety. A defect caught in an early ring reaches far fewer machines. Teams also have time to pull the update before it spreads further.
 Expired certificates 
 Illustration: Quartz
 An expired digital certificate can stop users from signing in to a cloud service even when its servers are running normally. On Feb. 3, 2020, Microsoft $MSFT attributed an outage of Microsoft Teams to an expired authentication certificate.
 That cause was a routine maintenance lapse, not a hardware fault or an attack. A certificate reached the end of its validity period. The systems that relied on it stopped trusting it, and people could not get into Teams.
 A digital certificate is a small file that ties a cryptographic key to a named identity, such as a website or an internal service. Software checks that certificate before it trusts the other side of a connection.
 Every certificate carries a start date and an end date. Once the end date passes, software that follows the standard rules treats the certificate as invalid and refuses the connection. A certificate that worked one minute can fail the next.
 Expiration dates exist on purpose. They limit how long a stolen or compromised key stays useful to an attacker. They also force organizations to reissue certificates on a regular schedule. Each renewal is a chance to update the underlying cryptography.
 Authentication certificates play a specific role inside cloud platforms. Services can use them to sign and verify the tokens that prove a user has logged in. When one expires, those tokens can no longer be validated. The sign-in step then fails for everyone who depends on it.
 Large cloud providers run many certificates across many services and teams. Each one has its own renewal date. A single missed renewal can block access to a product that is otherwise working.
 The standard defense is certificate tracking. Operators keep an inventory of every certificate in use, along with its owner and expiration date. Monitoring tools send alerts weeks ahead of an expiry. That gives a team time to renew the certificate and deploy a replacement.
 Automation reduces the reliance on calendars and memory. The ACME protocol lets servers request and install new certificates without manual steps. Let's Encrypt, a nonprofit certificate authority, built its service around ACME. It has issued certificates valid for 90 days, a short lifetime meant to push users toward automated renewal.
 Recovery from this type of outage usually means issuing a fresh certificate and pushing it to every system that needs it. The repair is a renewal rather than a rebuild. How long it takes depends on how many systems must receive the new certificate.
 DNS and BGP routing failures 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A service can keep running normally and still disappear from the internet if routing or DNS breaks. On Oct. 4, 2021, Meta $META 's services went offline after a configuration change on its backbone routers led to BGP route withdrawals, according to Meta .
 Two systems sit at the center of that incident. DNS, the Domain Name System, turns a name typed into a browser or app into the numerical IP address a computer needs to connect. BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is how separate networks across the internet tell one another which addresses they can reach and by which path.
 When a network announces routes through BGP, other networks learn how to send traffic to it. When those routes are withdrawn, the rest of the internet loses its directions. The servers behind those routes may still be powered on and working. Traffic has no path to reach them.
 Meta described a second step that widened the problem. Its DNS servers took themselves offline because they could not reach its data centers. With those servers gone, outside devices could not look up the addresses for Meta 's services at all.
 DNS failures also spread in a specific way. Devices and internet providers cache DNS answers for a set period, known as the time to live. Once a cached record expires, the next lookup has to go back to the authoritative servers. If those servers are offline, the lookup fails.
 This incident belongs to Meta , not Microsoft $MSFT , and it did not involve Outlook. It illustrates a cause that applies to any large provider. Every cloud service, including email platforms, depends on DNS and BGP so that users can find it.
 One common safeguard is out-of-band access. This is a separate management network, independent of the production network, that lets engineers reach and reconfigure routers when the main network is down. Without it, a bad routing change can cut off the same remote tools needed to reverse it.
 DDoS attacks 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A distributed denial-of-service attack knocks a service offline by burying it in more requests than it can answer. Real users then cannot get through. In June 2023, Microsoft $MSFT said disruptions to Outlook.com, OneDrive and the Azure portal came from layer 7 DDoS attacks.
 Microsoft attributed those attacks to a group it tracks as Storm-1359. The episode shows an outage caused by an outside party rather than by an internal mistake.
 The word "distributed" describes where the traffic comes from. An attacker directs many machines at once, often hijacked devices or rented servers spread across different networks. Blocking one address does little when many others keep sending.
 The "layer 7" label comes from the Open Systems Interconnection model, a seven-layer framework for describing how network communication works. Layer 7 is the application layer. That is where websites, webmail and APIs receive and respond to requests.
 Some DDoS attacks work lower in that stack and try to clog a network connection with sheer volume. Application-layer attacks take a different route. They send requests that resemble ordinary user activity, such as loading a page or asking for data.
 Each of those requests can force a server to run code, query a database or assemble a response. That makes answering them expensive. A server can run out of capacity before the network link itself fills up.
 The resemblance to real traffic makes this kind of attack hard to stop. Defenders have to separate automated requests from genuine users without locking out legitimate customers in the process.
 Defenses are software too, and they can fail. Microsoft said a DDoS attack hit Azure in July 2024. It also said an error in the implementation of its own defenses made the impact worse instead of limiting it.
 Large providers rely on traffic filtering to keep these floods away from the systems that do the work. Rate limiting caps how many requests a single source can send in a set period. Web application firewalls inspect incoming requests and drop ones that match known attack patterns. Content delivery networks spread incoming traffic across many locations. That way, no single site absorbs all of it.
 For someone trying to read email, a DDoS-driven outage looks much like any other failure. Pages stall, messages fail to load and requests time out.
 Sign-in failures 
 Illustration: Quartz
 When the system that checks who you are stops working, every service behind it can become unreachable, even while those services keep running normally. That happened on March 15, 2021, when an Azure Active Directory outage blocked sign-ins to many Microsoft $MSFT services.
 Microsoft attributed the outage to an error in an internal process that removed a signing key. Outlook and Teams were among the services reported as affected.
 Azure Active Directory is Microsoft 's cloud identity service, and Microsoft renamed it Microsoft Entra ID in 2023. It handles sign-in for Microsoft 365 apps. It also handles sign-in for many third-party applications that businesses connect to it. One identity system in front of many apps simplifies access for users and administrators. It also means a single fault in that layer can reach all of those apps at once.
 Sign-in systems of this kind issue a digital token after a user proves who they are. A token works like a stamped pass. The identity service signs it with a cryptographic key. Each app checks that signature before letting the user in.
 If the key an app expects is no longer available, the app cannot confirm that the pass is genuine. It rejects the request, even when the user typed the correct password.
 That distinction helps explain some cases of Outlook being down. Mailbox servers can store and deliver mail without trouble while the sign-in step fails. From the outside, users still see an error. The outage looks much the same as a failure in the mail servers themselves.
 Identity providers rotate signing keys on a schedule, retiring old keys and putting new ones in their place. Rotation is a routine security practice. It limits the damage if a key is ever exposed. The risk sits in the handoff. A key removed too early, or by mistake, can break sign-in for every app that still relies on it.
 Providers reduce this risk by building redundancy into the identity layer. That can mean running the service across multiple regions. It can mean keeping a retiring key published while apps switch to its replacement. It can also mean adding checks that stop an automated process from deleting a key that is still in use.
 Organizations that depend on a single identity provider can plan for sign-in disruptions too. One step is deciding in advance how staff will communicate if workplace apps become unreachable. Another is knowing where the provider posts incident updates, so administrators can confirm whether a sign-in failure is local or part of a wider outage.
 Server capacity limits 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Every server runs under hard ceilings set in its software, and crossing one can stop a service cold. On Nov. 25, 2020, Amazon $AMZN Web Services had a major outage in its us-east-1 region. AWS said adding capacity pushed its Kinesis front-end servers past an operating-system limit on the number of threads.
 The trigger was a step meant to help. Adding servers is usually how a provider keeps a service healthy under heavy load. Here, AWS said, that step itself crossed the limit.
 Amazon Kinesis is the AWS service for collecting and processing streaming data in real time. Front-end servers sit at the edge of a service like this. They receive incoming requests and hand them to the systems that do the underlying work.
 A thread is a single sequence of instructions that a computer runs. A program can run many threads at once to handle many tasks in parallel. Operating systems cap how many threads can exist at the same time. That cap protects the machine from exhausting its memory and other resources.
 When a program tries to go beyond that ceiling, the operating system refuses to create more threads. Software that depends on those threads can then fail to do its job. A limit that normal operation never reaches can sit unnoticed until growth runs into it.
 The damage did not stay inside Kinesis. AWS said many of its services that depended on Kinesis were affected. Cloud platforms build services on top of other services. A single failing component can reach well beyond its own function.
 This was an AWS incident, and it did not involve Microsoft $MSFT 's systems. It shows a type of failure that any large cloud platform can face.
 Providers guard against this kind of outage by watching how close their systems run to configured limits, not just whether they are up. Tracking thread counts, open file handles and memory use against their ceilings gives engineers warning before a scaling step crosses one. Engineers can also review the operating-system defaults their software relies on and raise them deliberately where growth requires it.
 Automated scaling and cascading failures 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Automated scaling can take down cloud services when the systems around it react in ways their designers did not predict. Amazon $AMZN Web Services described that pattern after a large outage in its us-east-1 region, based in Northern Virginia, on Dec. 7, 2021.
 AWS said an automated activity to scale a service in its main network caused unexpected behavior from many clients inside its internal network. That behavior led to congestion. The congestion landed on the networking devices that link AWS's internal network to its main network.
 Those devices carry traffic between the two networks. When they become congested, traffic crossing between the networks slows or stalls. Systems on either side that need to talk to each other then start to time out.
 Engineers call this pattern a cascading failure. One component falters, and the load or errors it produces push neighboring components past their own limits. Each new failure adds pressure somewhere else, and the damage grows step by step.
 Retries can speed up the spiral. When a client gets no response, it often sends the same request again. If a large number of clients retry at the same moment, the extra traffic deepens the congestion that caused the delays in the first place.
 Automation raises the stakes because it acts at machine speed. Scaling systems exist to add or remove capacity faster than a human operator could. That same speed means an unexpected side effect can spread across a network before anyone has diagnosed it.
 A common defense is throttling. A throttled service caps how many requests it accepts from a client in a given window and turns away the rest. Clients, in turn, can be built to back off. Exponential backoff makes each retry wait longer than the one before. Adding random jitter keeps clients from retrying in lockstep.
 Engineers also use circuit breakers, which stop calls to a struggling dependency for a period so it has room to recover. Each of these tools accepts a small number of rejected requests in exchange for keeping the wider system stable.
 The December 2021 incident was an Amazon outage, not a Microsoft $MSFT one. It shows how an automated action inside one provider can ripple outward. Large cloud platforms that scale themselves automatically face the same kind of risk.
 Data center cooling failures 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Cloud services can go down when a data center cannot get rid of the heat its servers produce. On July 19, 2022, during a heat wave in London, Google $GOOGL Cloud and Oracle $ORCL both reported cooling-related problems at London facilities. Both providers tied the trouble to hot weather that overwhelmed cooling and affected equipment.
 Every server turns the electricity it uses into heat. Thousands of machines packed into rows of racks can raise the temperature of a room quickly if that heat is not carried away. For a data center, cooling is as essential as power and network connections.
 Most facilities remove heat in stages. Air or liquid draws heat away from the servers. Equipment such as chillers, cooling towers or dry coolers then releases it outdoors. That last step works best when the outside air is much cooler than the air or water carrying the heat.
 A heat wave squeezes that margin. As outdoor temperatures rise, cooling equipment has a harder time shedding heat. Demand from the servers does not fall to match. The cooling system ends up working hardest at the moment it is least able to keep up.
 Servers have built-in protections against overheating. Processors slow themselves down when they run hot, and hardware can switch off to avoid permanent damage. Operators may also power down some machines on purpose to keep the rest of a room within safe limits. Each of those steps can slow or stop customer workloads.
 The London problems involved two separate providers on the same day. Both were linked to the same hot weather. A configuration error or a faulty update starts with a single decision inside a company. Weather is an outside condition, and it can strain many facilities in the same city at once.
 Cooling systems are sized for the conditions a site expects to face. A heat wave beyond that range can push equipment past what it was built to handle.
 Providers reduce the risk through climate design. That means building cooling with spare capacity and planning for hotter conditions than a site normally sees. Redundant cooling units let one unit fail without the room overheating. Large cloud platforms also split regions into separate zones. Customers can run copies of their systems in more than one location. A problem at one facility then does not have to take a whole service down.
 When a website or app is unavailable on an unusually hot day, the cause may sit in a building's mechanical plant rather than in its software.
 Power failures 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Power problems can take down a cloud region even when its servers, software and network have no faults of their own. On Sept. 4, 2018, lightning strikes near Microsoft $MSFT Azure's South Central U.S. region in San Antonio caused a voltage spike that disrupted Azure services.
 Microsoft said the spike knocked cooling systems offline at the site. It said equipment then shut down automatically to protect itself. The failure moved from the electrical system to the cooling plant and finally to the computing hardware.
 A voltage spike, also called a surge, is a brief jump in voltage above the level that equipment is designed to handle. Lightning does not need to hit a building directly to cause one. A strike on or near power lines can send a surge through the grid into connected facilities.
 Data centers use several layers of electrical protection to guard against these events. Surge protection devices divert excess voltage away from sensitive equipment. Uninterruptible power supplies, usually built around large battery banks, keep systems running through short interruptions. Diesel generators start up to carry the load during longer utility outages.
 Each layer covers a different kind of failure. Batteries bridge the seconds before generators reach full output. Generators handle a sustained loss of grid power. Surge protection deals with spikes that backup power alone cannot absorb.
 Cooling depends on electricity as much as servers do. Chillers, pumps and fans all need a steady supply. Without them, hardware temperatures climb quickly. Automatic shutdowns exist to prevent heat damage that could take far longer to repair.
 The reach of a site-level event depends on how services are spread out. Cloud providers organize infrastructure into regions, which are geographic areas containing one or more data centers. Workloads that run in a single region rely on that region's facilities staying up.
 Applications built across several regions can shift traffic elsewhere when one location fails. That design costs more and adds complexity, and not every customer uses it. Outlook.com and Exchange Online run on Microsoft 's own cloud infrastructure. The data centers behind them depend on the same kinds of power and cooling systems.
 Providers reduce power risk through regular generator testing, redundant utility feeds and surge protection that covers both power and cooling systems. Weather remains outside their control. Lightning, storms and grid failures are physical events that no software fix can prevent.
